To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the required server bandwidth is an inadequate quality of service metric for scalable on-demand streaming systems and that the required server capacity is a more accurate metric.

(a) the previously defined "required server bandwidths" for scalable streaming protocols are insufficient to ensure low client waiting times or balking rates, (b) the new models developed here can be used to determine the required server bandwidth for a given target balking rate, and (c) for high to moderately loaded media servers, a 10 -50% increase in server bandwidth is needed over that defined by previous work.

for a scalable media server to provide good service to a large number of clients, its required server bandwidth must be increased by a factor of 10 - 1000 compared to the bandwidth needed to support a single client".
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design and analysis of a new class of scalable media servers.
the design and evaluation of quality of service for on-demand media streaming systems.
the design of scalable media servers that provide high quality of service to the clients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the "required server" bandwidth metric is useful, but only if the server is well-provisioned to handle a client load that is 10% greater or more than the expected load.

, for scalable media servers that provide immediate service, it is important to consider both mean wait and balking rate, and that the required server bandwidth defined in previous work should be augmented with the additional requirement that the balking rate should be acceptably low.

, for scalable on-demand media servers that provide immediate service during periods of non-overload, a simple and accurate analytic model can be constructed that can be used by a media server designer to select the server bandwidth needed, given the anticipated number of media files (or total file size), client access frequency, and desired client balking rate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a well-designed media server should be configured with a bandwidth that exceeds the required server bandwidth by at least 50% in order to achieve very low client waiting time and low balking rates.

a scalable media server that is configured with the "Required Server Bandwidth" defined in previous research may provide good service quality (i.e., very low mean client wait) to a client base that has an anticipated total request rate that is 10% or less than the anticipated load, but may have un-acceptably high client balk rates if the actual client request rate is more than 5% greater than anticipated.
the "required server capacity" for a scalable media server should be defined as that which achieves the desired balking rate, and not as that which achieves some desired mean wait.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, when evaluating a media server, one should not only consider the server bandwidth, but also the client balking rate, which is a measure of the quality of service perceived by the clients.

the required server bandwidth defined in previous work is not a useful metric for assessing the quality of service of a scalable media server, and that a new metric is needed that reflects the mean wait and balking rate.
a scalable on-demand media server should be configured with a server bandwidth at least 10 - 100% greater than the "required server capacity" defined in previous studies.
